lines: Missing pages worry me less than people who never read warnings.
Villages remember more than people expect.
Ink is quiet until someone needs proof.
Records do not care who feels embarrassed by them.
A tidy shelf is proof that peace can be arranged, briefly.
Forgotten warnings do not become kinder. They become <jump>surprises</jump>.
Most days, I am at the lectern, trying to keep records and rumors from becoming everyone else's problem.
People think record-keeping is simple until something goes wrong and suddenly it is very important.
A village runs on small work. Nobody praises it until it stops happening.
I trust a good quill more than a loud promise. The quill has less to prove.
You may prefer I forget. I have chosen a profession that argues otherwise.
I have seen bad sources with more sense than that.
Careful. Even ink looks softer than your manners right now.
You walk in like trouble forgot to close the door behind it.
I have seen broken record-keeping with better instincts than you.
Careful. The village has long memories and very little patience today.
You are not as frightening as you think. That may be the problem.
If foolishness made noise, you would drown out the bell.
Do not test me just because I am speaking in complete sentences.
Your confidence is <shake>louder</shake> than your sense.
The story of me following you needs editing. Mostly shorter chapters and fewer hazards.
I remember following you through that road. My feet remember it even better.
That trip across that road taught me to ask more questions before walking.
Following you taught me that plans sound much safer before anyone starts walking.
I kept up, mostly. My feet have a harsher opinion of the trip.
Next time, warn me before the road becomes a test of character.
I learned two things out there: stay close, and ask better questions earlier.
You move like danger is a normal part of the route. I am still adjusting to that.
It was not all bad. Some views are worth sore legs and nervous glances.
If I followed you again, I would pack more food and fewer assumptions.
The boat chapter of our journey was damp, brief, and badly footnoted.
That boat trip still sits oddly in my memory, but at least it floated.
A boat can make a bad plan quieter. It can't make me forget it.

Every village has a history. Some of it even waits politely on shelves.
Books are quiet until you need them. Then they become everyone who wrote before you.
I keep records because memory without witnesses starts bargaining with itself.
Most days, I am at the lectern, trying to keep records and rumors from becoming everyone else's problem.

If you want my honest answer, slow down first. Rushed questions usually hide worse ones.
The village looks calm from a distance. Up close, it is mostly chores arguing with weather.
I notice the little things. That is either a skill or what the lectern has done to me.
